Abstract. In the context of great global attention to energy security, the development and utilization 
of renewable energy have become a key measure to achieve the goal of high-quality development 
and "two-carbon." Our work is to study the ecological impact of HPC analysis. Three different 
machine learning models — Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest, and Gradient 
Boosting—are employed in this study to predict utilization rates based on factors like energy mix and 
workload characteristics. An ARIMA (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) model forecasts 
future energy consumption trends based on historical data from different data center types 
(Traditional, Cloud, and Hyperscale). These analyses show a worrying increase trend in energy use 
and carbon emissions. In addition, a SARIMA (Seasonal ARIMA) model is fitted to forecast future 
energy consumption over various economic sectors (residential, commercial, and industrial), 
including historical trends and seasonality. That enables a more complete analysis of the entire 
energy landscape and how it is weighed toward HPC. The model analyzes several future energy mix 
scenarios, from a gradually maintained role of fossil fuels to rapidly increasing adoption of 
renewables. The study estimates the possible contributions of increasing renewable penetration to 
reducing HPC's carbon footprint. 
Keywords: Electricity Consumption Estimation; Carbon Emission Prediction; Time Series Analysis. 
1. Introduction 
HPC is essential in science and engineering because it provides a system that connects user data 
to supercomputers with high usability and efficiency. HPC is highly dependent on nonrenewable 
energy sources, so it may seriously impact the natural environment, polluting various resources. 
The operation of HPCS and large data centers consumes large amounts of water and chemical 
coolants to cope with the heat generated by these systems. These cooling measures are essential to 
ensure the continued operation of the facilities. However, the need for regular coolant replacement 
has led to wastewater contamination issues. 
Furthermore, due to the inherent component aging, computing power will inevitably decline, so 
HPC hardware needs to be replaced over time. This replacement will lead to issues related to e-waste, 
as this HPC hardware will be complicated to degrade naturally in the ecosystem without effective 
disposal. Moreover, manufacturing these HPC hardware components can also contribute to these 
problems, as electronic components become potential sources of e-waste. 
Considering its importance in HPC data center operations, we expand to include water usage and 
significant cooling. In support of this focus, the authors note the high water use of these structures, 
which occupy regions of water stress in the case of many. They construct a linear statistical model 
for forecasting future water consumption, providing additional evidence for HPC expansion's 
environmental implications. 
To conclude, we provide practical recommendations to mitigate the HPC environmental footprint. 
These suggestions include technical solutions (e.g., efficient use of data centers, design of more 
energy-conserving hardware, and optimization of cooling systems) as well as policy-based solutions

2. Problem Restatement 
A model aimed at identifying and predicting the impact of the development of data centers using 
high-performance computing hardware will be implemented to determine the extent to which the 
development of such centers affects environmental conditions. In particular, the model will 
encompass the following elements: 
Considering the data center's operation (in full and average operation mode), the annual electricity 
consumption will be used to determine a model capable of simulating the consequences of its energy 
consumption in its environment. The model will pay attention to carbon emissions into the 
atmosphere. 
The model will be able to predict future environmental impact trends by embedding predictions of 
the growth of HPC hardware use. It will be able to predict the actual scale of the environmental impact 
in 2030. 
We will consider replacing traditional nonrenewable and waste-producing energies with more 
sustainable renewable energies, among other things. The model should be designed to account for 
cooling system carbon emissions and the environmental impact of cooling system disposal. 
It is also assumed that a series of steps or activities that could reduce the environmental impact of 
data center operations are now in use. Based on this assumption, the model can reflect this mitigation 
of environmental influences. 
Finally, based on this model and its outputs, please write an essay for the UN Advisory Board 
proposing adding the model outputs as a section to their report on AI in which the environmental 
consequences of HPC employed for AI computation are discussed. 
3. Models and Results 
3.1 Utilization Rate of Different HPC Centers 
HPC centers are different from each other. They encompass every level, from small-scale clusters 
in research benches to massive hyper-scale data centers powering AI training and computationally 
demanding tasks. In our work, HPC centers are divided into three categories by scale and application, 
including traditional, hyperscale, and cloud. Energy utilization rate is a key factor affecting HPC's 
energy consumption. The utilization rates of different types of HPC centers are changing along with 
the development of technology. This section predicts the future utilization rates of three different 
types of HPC centers.

Figure 1 displays the analysis of energy utilization which incorporates both historical data and 
ARIMA model prognostications. The historical energy utilization trends from 2015 to 2021 decline 
steadily as shown through the blue line. The orange dotted line in Figure one represents the imagined 
in-sample data from the ARIMA model that overlaps effectively with previously recorded values. 
The forecasted periods of 2022-2025 are displayed through the green dashed line in the forecast done 
by the ARIMA model. According to the forecast the decrease in energy utilization will continue but 
plateau at a stable energy consumption level for a brief period before this adjustment. The forecast 
shows a follow-up reduction in energy utilization which proceeds at a slow pace while remaining 
minimal. 
Therefore, according to the ARIMA model, the downward trend of energy utilization is expected 
to slow compared to the past. The forecast stabilizes at a relatively constant level of energy utilization 
in future years, suggesting that the development of Hyperscale and Cloud computing will gradually 
replace Traditional data centers. It will significantly alleviate the pressure of increasing demand for 
HPC on energy consumption.

3.2.1 Granger Causality Test 
After preprocessing and ensuring the data is stationary, we perform Granger Causality tests to 
assess whether one variable's past values can help predict another variable's future values. Specifically, 
we examine the following relationships: 
The hypothesis tested in Granger Causality is: 
Null Hypothesis (H₀): Past values of X do not Granger cause Y. 
Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): Past values of X Granger cause Y. 
That will help us understand if the energy mix (especially the renewable and low carbon 
percentages) has a lagged impact on carbon intensity.

Fig 4. Carbon emission per unit of electricity consumption 
Figure 4 represents a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) with a Gaussian family to study the 
association of carbon emissions from electricity generation and renewable energy share in the energy 
mix and year. The abscissa is time (year), and the ordinate is carbon emission of electricity. Points in

shows the estimated values from the GLM in terms of carbon emissions. The filled orange band 
surrounding the regression line shows the 95% confidence as bounds on the model's predictions, 
reflecting the uncertainty of the model estimates. 
The findings indicate an overall downward trend in carbon emissions from electricity production 
for the period examined. GLM can capture this trend, and the predicted values accurately align with 
the observed data values. The downward trend reflects that the increase in renewable energy usage is 
associated with reducing carbon emissions in the electricity sector. Nevertheless, exploring if causal 
relationships exist in another study would be necessary. The confidence interval width indicates a 
level of uncertainty in the model's predictions, which is not necessarily surprising, especially at the 
start and end of the data. The overall monotonic decline combined with higher and higher shares of 
renewables indicates a possible correlation between renewable energy use and lower carbon 
emissions in the electricity sector.

Fig 5. Partial regression plot 
In Figure 6, each subplot illustrates the relationship between the response variable and one 
predictor. The x-axis of every subplot is the partial residuals of the predictor, i.e., the portion of the 
predictor regressor that is not captured by the other predictor variables. On the y-axis, the partial 
residuals of the response variable are shown, that is, the residual part of the response, which the other 
predictors do not explain. The black line appearing in each plot is the regressive line of the respective 
predictor, indicating the direction and severity of the linear association of this predictor with the 
response. 
These partial regression plots allow for the importance of each predictor variable to be teased out 
in the context of the response variable while keeping the other predictors fixed. They allow a visual 
presentation of the relationships found by the GLM and can assist in finding any non-linearity or 
peculiar behavior in the data. 
 
Fig 6. Distribution of residuals and Q-Q plot of residuals 
Figure 7 displays diagnostic plots for assessing the residuals. The histogram is unimodal (with one 
peak) and slightly skewed. Most residuals are clustered around zero, with a few more significant 
positive residuals causing the tail to the right. The histogram does not perfectly conform to the 
standard curve, implying a slight departure from normality, but it is not extreme. The right skew is 
the main departure. The y-axis "Count" shows how many residuals are found in each bin. The upper 
bar represents that the residuals are roughly concentrated between 0.0025 and 0.01. 
In the Q-Q plot of residuals, points are more or less aligned with the diagonal red line, suggesting 
a good alignment with a normal distribution. Nevertheless, the point representing the extreme left 
corner deviates from the line, implying the possible outlier or an even slightly heavier left tail than in 
an ideal normal distribution. The points at the upper right also deviate, hinting at a slight right skew. 
Residuals have a satisfactory approximation of normal distribution; however, it is not perfect. The 
main discrepancies are the slight right skew and possible outlier, as demonstrated by the Q-Q plot.

As the global HPC energy consumption model has shown, the trend has a worrying pattern. By 
combining Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), capacity prediction, and various 
machine learning models (linear regression, Polynomial Regression, Support Vector Regression, 
Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting), we have studied capacity prediction and utilization rate 
prediction with daily observation data from 2021 to 2023 from five major countries. Our results 
suggest a significant and growing energy consumption by HPC infrastructure based on increasing 
capacity and utilization.

Abstract: In the context of great global attention to energy security, the development and utilization of renewable energy have become a key measure to achieve the goal of high-quality development and "two-carbon." Our work is to study the ecological impact of HPC analysis. Three different machine learning models — Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting—are employed in this study to predict utilization rates based on factors like energy mix and workload characteristics. An ARIMA (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) model forecasts future energy consumption trends based on historical data from different data center types (Traditional, Cloud, and Hyperscale). These analyses show a worrying increase trend in energy use and carbon emissions. In addition, a SARIMA (Seasonal ARIMA) model is fitted to forecast future energy consumption over various economic sectors (residential, commercial, and industrial), including historical trends and seasonality. That enables a more complete analysis of the entire energy landscape and how it is weighed toward HPC. The model analyzes several future energy mix scenarios, from a gradually maintained role of fossil fuels to rapidly increasing adoption of renewables. The study estimates the possible contributions of increasing renewable penetration to reducing HPC's carbon footprint.
